surfaces.part: striped awning (orange/white stripes with a scalloped lower edge)

answer.evidence: Rows 3-7 are a striped awning plane (orange at x=8, white at x=12). Its scalloped lower edge is at row 7, and a dark eave-shadow line follows at row 8, which meets evidence (c). Below it, rows 9-15 are a cream shop front with shelf bands, about 7 rows tall. The row 1-2 strip and the left post are vertical faces, and the post is a minor part. The awning could be read as a front-facing valance, but the stripe block with an edge line and shadow below it is enough for a top plane.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate on the board is only a tiny fragment, roughly 14x18 source pixels, with a white/orange block and a dark outline. It does not read as a whole building. There is no visible roof, wall or door structure at the reference scale, so it doesn't match the building kind of the two references. The references show many-tile scalloped roofs with per-tile highlights, timber framing, plaster speckle and stone shaded one by one, about 5-6 steps per material. The candidate shows only about 3 steps per material and no roof-tile scallops or stone or plaster texture. The measured facts (12 visible tones, 0% near-flat, 0% neutral dark edges) are on par with the references. But the picture shows a small, simple object with far less visible structure and information than the buildings next to it, and the 12 tones probably come from a few distinct areas rather than rich shading. The outline looks tinted, not near-black. The piece fails because it is not a complete building with a roof, walls and door and has much less content than the references.

surfaces.part: cream wall / counter ledge below awning

answer.evidence: Rows 3-7 are a striped awning plane (orange stripe at x=8, white at x=12). It ends in a darker scalloped edge at row 7 with a dark outline at row 8, which acts as the front edge and eave shadow. Below it is a cream front face at rows 9-15, with a ledge line at rows 10-11. A wooden post runs down the left side as a vertical face. The awning gives 5 rows of top surface above 7 rows of front face, so the main body is read as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny sprite, about one tile, at the far right of the board. The references are full houses several tiles wide, with a scalloped tile roof, timber-and-plaster or stone walls, and a door. The candidate does not read as a whole building with roof, walls, door and windows. It looks closer to a small sign or icon, so the kind does not match. The facts show only 12 distinct colours for the whole piece, against 185 and 66 for the references. Its 12 visible tones in one tile equal the reference tile, but that is the entire piece's palette. It is spread across a single tile and cannot carry the per-material ramps (roof highlight/light/mid/dark/deep, plaster speckle, stone-by-stone shading) that the references show. The edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted rather than black, which is fine. There are no flat 5x5 fills, but at this size that says little. Overall it is far thinner and less developed than the references as a building, so it fails.
